Don't skimp on the group activities. As long as you trust the teachers/tutors, group classes can be incredible learning opportunities. It's not just for team sports! That said, definitely keep the basis of the curriculum rooted at home.

Talk to your local library about how they can help - membership = free books (nonfiction and fiction) but also many libraries now subscribe to multiple electronic resources/databases which can be amazing as well as safer then letting kids search the internet freely (especially image databases!).

The big difference for homeschool as compared to school is you can nuture a childs natural love of learning rather than creating a hate for learning. Find something your kid is interested in and go from there until they are bored then move on. Kid likes dinosaurs? That's great - dinosaurs can cover biology, social structures, habitat, archeology, history, myth, legends, literature, astronomy, geography, geology etc. etc.

Don't skimp on the social stuff but it is isn't necessary to have all socialisation with peers of exact age. Socialising with older kids and adults are great for setting examples, maturing and learning but socialising with younger kids helps empathy and learning how to teach others. Try homeschooling groups, church groups, sports, library, museums, galleries, fetes, festivals, open days at farms and historic places etc.

I was homeschooled all my school years by my mom. She lived by the motto the less $$ you spend, the better education. Whereas our friends were dropping $$$ on each kid a year, Momma would buy used books and pay to borrow a set of Sonlight readers from a friend. We used the Library a lot!

My parents had plenty of money, and they did buy consumable books new as well as other high quality school books, but they never got into the whole “slave to one curriculum” stuff many of my friends got stuck in. That worked out great for me since when I would hate a textbook my mom would listen to me and we’d find something else since there wasn’t a lot of sunk cost.

First, congratulations on your impending bundle of joy! :D That's exciting.

Okay. So it really helps to have some kind of a schedule. Some people like family organizers. I like to get one of those big "made for moms" calendars with extra-huge squares, and write out my entire year's lessons so I know exactly what to do every single day. It helps me make sure we're on track. When your kids are tiny and just starting out, you don't need a very rigid structure, or a million subjects - you want to do math and language arts every day, and then add in things like reading and science and art a few times a week. You will have probably one to two hours tops in which they'll be able to focus and then their attention wanders. My kids learned to read and print during our kindergarten year; for first grade we focused on honing those skills. They don't need too much beyond that. Basic math, basic science, easy stuff.

We used Pathway Readers with our kids for first and second grades and they are fantastic - you can use them as just a reading course, or you can use it as a full language arts curriculum. They're very sweet and they are meant for kids who are either brand new readers or who have not yet learned to read. As you read through the book, the language slowly becomes more complex as their reading skills improve. They tell stories about life on a Mennonite farm, which my kids loved. We have also used Christian Light Education books for many years and they're excellent! Their math is well put together and your kids will definitely get a solid math education. Their language arts is also excellent. Their science...no! Not unless you think "it rains because God sends the rain" qualifies as science. ;) I am a Christian but I still thought that was lame. If you are interested in free resources, check out the Khan Academy - it is AWESOME! I'm not sure what they offer at the first grade level because we didn't start using it until this school year (seventh and eighth grade), but it's worth a look.

Get involved with a local homeschool group if you can find one that isn't too full of crazies. ;) You will need the support and encouragement! And look at interesting places nearby that you can visit with the kids...a field trip once a month can be a really cool way to do school too.
Thank you! And thank you for all the advice.

If you're having fun with your kid, you're probably doing it right. Lots of rewards/positive reinforcement, our kids are rewarded for all of the work they do. Don't buy into the popular idea that the kid will somehow know what's in his best interest. It's just a matter of choosing the right subjects, and making them fun (by getting yourself involved) and rewarding.
